add.issue.name: xlint: check final newline in .md files

edit.description.md:
## Problem

`check_final_newline` runs only in the `.py` branch of `check_file` in `tools/xlint/xlint.py`. A `.md` file gets exactly one check (space indentation), so a missing final newline in Markdown is invisible to xlint.

Hit live 2026-09-27: an edit silently dropped the trailing newline from `.agents/agent-notes-secretary-3.md`. Three sibling notes files all end with a newline, so it was a regression rather than house style — and xlint reported the file clean.

## Scope

- Apply `check_final_newline` to the `.md` branch, under the existing `--no-final-newline` flag.
- Respect the existing fence/frontmatter exemptions where relevant.

## Acceptance

- A `.md` missing its trailing newline fails; one with it passes.
- `--no-final-newline` disables the check for `.md` as it does for `.py`.
- Repo-wide `xlint $(git ls-files '*.md')` is clean, or every remaining finding is dispositioned.

## Notes

- **ai-ok**: an AI may pick this up and implement it without extensive discussion with the human.
- Related: GBNEWPS (frontmatter + fenced-code exemptions) is already implemented in `ed3d27e` but still sits in Todo — that ticket's status looks stale.
- Adjacent, deliberately *not* in scope: `check_trailing_whitespace` is also language-independent and is `.py`-only today. Worth its own ticket.

add.issue.name: Replace the broken coding subagent (mimo) — evaluate nemotron-3-ultra vs north-mini-code for quality

edit.description.md:
`opencode/mimo-v2.5-free` — the model AGENTS.md assigns to coding via `dispatch coding` — **fails instantly** with an opaque `UnknownError` ("Unexpected server error", ref `err_87964db6`, `err_0ac8beb6`). Tried twice on 2026-09-27, not transient; the process never starts. Coding work had to be run on `opencode/nemotron-3-ultra-free` instead, which worked 3/3.

**The evaluation, per the human (2026-09-27):** compare quality of
- `opencode/nemotron-3-ultra-free` — in effect **very cheap**: generous limits, *not*
  bundled into the same pool as big-pickle (unlike mimo and some others), and not
  in the OpenRouter free pool either. So mimo was effectively a *third* generous pool.
- `openrouter/cohere/north-mini-code:free` — a coding specialist (30B MoE, 3B active,
  256K ctx, quality 24). Currently referenced in 5 agent files: `mechanic.md`,
  `programmer.md`, `overseer.md`, `worker-mimo.md`, `worker-north-mini-code.md`.

**Cost asymmetry to weigh:** north-mini-code sits on the **shared OpenRouter `:free`
pool**, which AGENTS.md says to reserve for models with no console equivalent. When
that daily pool hits zero every `:free` model returns empty and everything looks
broken. nemotron-ultra is on opencode's console gateway with generous limits. So
north-mini-code is not merely pricier in tokens — it is on a failure-prone pool.

**The deciding question is quality, because cheapness wins ties.** Cheapness per run
does not compensate for errors, so: given no meaningful change in quality, a cheaper
model is better. That makes this a quality comparison first and a cost comparison
second, with the pool-reliability difference as the tiebreak.

**Method note:** a real quality comparison needs a task with a known-correct answer
and scored output, not a vibe check. The cursor-reviewer-skill trials in
`/storage/cursor-review-baseline/` are the existing precedent for a scored,
frozen-subject comparison — reuse that shape rather than inventing one.

Also settle `programmer.md`'s model pin (see `WV26JZ2`, `3RVME3H`): it names
`worker-north-mini-code` while AGENTS.md's dispatch table says `worker-mimo`, and
the programmer is supposed to delegate coding to a worker anyway.

add.issue.name: Off-vocabulary categories in tasks.csv: research / ai-docs / personal (#61–#63, #65, #66)

edit.description.md:
Five open tasks carry category values that were never ruled on. All five appeared on 2026-09-27, all from the model-benchmark / codebase-comprehension work, and they are the only rows in the entire store that use them.

| # | category | task |
|---|----------|------|
| 61 | `research` | Model benchmark: widen the episode set |
| 62 | `ai-docs` | Correct library/ai/free-model-tier-list.md |
| 63 | `research` | Model benchmark: set G2–G5 thresholds |
| 65 | `personal` | Codebase comprehension learning process |
| 66 | `personal` | First 45-min comprehension block on mms-frontend |

## Why this needs a ruling, not a cleanup

The category column is the membership axis for project-scoped views (SPEC R4, Decision 8). A category only earns its place if some `.taskview.yaml` can scope to it or a pane can ask for it. `research` and `ai-docs` are neither a project nor a life area — they are *activities*. They name what the task is being done for, not what it is about, and that distinction is exactly what the human's rule turns on: **category = what the work is about, not which repo you are sitting in** (SPEC Decision 17).

The deeper problem is accretion. Nothing rejects a new category value, so the vocabulary grows one task at a time, by whoever happens to be in a session. A column that widens silently stops being a vocabulary. It is the same free-text drift already recorded for tags (`verif` vs `verify`), one level up and slower to notice.

## The specific questions

**#61, #62, #63 — model benchmark.** Three defensible answers, genuinely different:

- `work` — `TASKS.md` files the model benchmark under `### Work`.
- `XLib` — the harness lives at `$XLIB/tools/modelbench/`. Precedent: #56 (taskview project-specific) was labelled `XLib` even though its plan lives in the Agents repo, for exactly this reason.
- `Agents` — the plan is `Agents/plans/model-benchmark.md`, the output is `Agents/library/ai/models/`.

`#56` already set the precedent, so `XLib` is the consistent answer unless the human rules the benchmark is work rather than tooling.

**#65, #66 — codebase comprehension.** Almost certainly the same thing as `Personal Development`, spelled differently — `personal` vs `Personal Development` is the `verif`/`verify` drift again. `Personal Development` is the `TASKS.md` section name and is what #22, #23 and #41 were just labelled with in the 2026-09-27 pass, so these two are the odd ones out.

## Left unchanged on purpose

A live session owns this work. Relabelling under it would be invisible to whoever is mid-task and would make the pane disagree with the plan they are reading. Needs the human's ruling first, then one `taskupdate.py update <id> --category ...` per task.

add.issue.name: Agents AGENTS.md: `dispatch coding` routes to a big-pickle-pool worker, and worker-mimo pins a model the console dropped

edit.description.md:
`/storage/Agents/AGENTS.md` contradicts itself on the one rule that exists to protect the main model's quota.

- `:139` — "The main model (big-pickle / nemotron-3-ultra-free) is the primary rate-limit bottleneck — **preserve it by offloading** non-trivial work to subagents."
- `:143` — "**Coding / implementation** → `worker-mimo` (console `opencode/mimo-v2.5-free`). Strong coder; **use for coding by default**."
- `:173`, `:221`, `:247` repeat the `worker-mimo` routing (secretary pattern, programmer role, mechanic role).

`mimo` is **pool 1 — it shares big-pickle's quota** (topology in `/storage/Agents/.agents/shared-notes.md`, "Rate-limit pool topology (2026-09-27)"). So the default coding route spends the quota the line above it says to preserve, and it *is* the default: every dispatched coding task takes it.

**It is also self-refuting in practice.** `:141` tells agents to get the worker from `python3 $XLIB/tools/agent-coord.py dispatch <category>` — and that command's WORKER_MAP (`tools/agent-coord.py:540`) returns **`worker-north-mini-code`**. XLib's own AGENTS.md was already fixed this way (`8cb4daf`, plus the WORKER_MAP fix, both committed). The Agents file is the one left behind: `worker-mimo.md`'s description was already updated ("dispatch coding currently maps to worker-north-mini-code") and its parent doc was not.

**Second, mechanical defect — the pin is stale.** `worker-mimo.md` pins `opencode/mimo-v2.5-free`. `opencode models` (verified 2026-09-27) no longer lists v2.5; it lists **`opencode/mimo-v2.6-flash-free`**. A pin to a model the provider dropped is a dead worker behind a live name — the shared rule already says "ALWAYS verify with `opencode models` before pinning a model ID in an agent file".

**Fix, two parts:**

1. Re-point the four routing lines in `/storage/Agents/AGENTS.md` to `worker-north-mini-code` — or to whatever `9J30DNW` settles — so the doc matches the tool it tells agents to run, and coding stops defaulting into the protected pool.
2. Re-point `worker-mimo.md`'s `model:` to `mimo-v2.6-flash-free`, or delete the agent if nothing routes to it any more. Do not leave a broken pin.

**Related, not duplicate.** `9J30DNW` decides *which model codes best* (mimo fails outright; nemotron-3-ultra vs north-mini-code on quality, with the shared OpenRouter `:free` pool as the cost tiebreak). This ticket is the rule-level contradiction plus a stale pin, and it does not need that comparison settled. If `9J30DNW` picks the worker, part 1 collapses to a one-line edit.

add.issue.name: tasks.csv header declares 5 columns while every new row carries 8 — header-driven readers mis-map silently

edit.description.md:
Found while auditing taskview after the category/tag rollout (2026-09-27).

**The defect.** `~/.local/share/taskview/tasks.csv` carries the *old* header line:

    id,status,title,due_ts,chg_ts

but the schema is 8 columns (`// Schema:` comment line says so) and `ensure_csv` in `tools/taskview/taskupdate.py:20` writes 8 when it creates a file. It no-ops when the file already exists, so the on-disk header never self-heals. Field census of the live file: 63 rows with 5 fields, 48 with 8, 7 with 6, the rest wider (quoted titles containing commas — those parse fine).

**Why it matters.** `taskupdate.py` itself reads *positionally* (`row[5]`, guarded by `len(row) >`), so the tool is correct. The trap is any **header-driven** reader: `csv.DictReader` trusts that line and silently puts `category` under `due_ts` and shifts everything after. That already cost one session a whole table it was building for the human. A quiet wrong answer is worse than a crash.

**Fix options, pick one.**
- Repair the header on open (rewrite the field-name line, and migrate the 5-field rows to 8 so the file stops being mixed-format).
- Or drop the header line entirely and treat position 5-8 as optional — the readers already guard with `len(row) >`.
- Or leave the data alone and add a `taskupdate.py migrate` that reports the mixed format without writing.

**Definition of done.** A reader built on the header agrees with a positional reader for every id in the file, and there is a test that fails on the current file. Needs a spec line + tests per `XLib/doc/development.md` — taskview is committed (`250aaf1`), so this is real code, not scratch.

Related: the `tasks.csv` duplication between taskview and this board is `JM8GVW8`; vocabulary drift in the same file is `SNXBR23`.

add.issue.name: taskview pane shows no task id — a task can only be named by its truncated title

edit.description.md:
Found 2026-09-27, from the human: *"Referring to tasks by ID is convenient, but I don't have a quick reference right now."*

**The gap.** The tmux task pane renders title only — `truncate(current['title'], width - 2)` at `tools/taskview/taskview.py:371` for the current task, `:389` for the UPCOMING list. No id appears anywhere, so the pane cannot answer "which one is this?" Two titles sharing a first few words are indistinguishable, and truncated titles are worse.

Concrete symptom from this session: asked whether `#40` was the task about part switching, the only handle available was the number — the title had been truncated out of recognition.

**Proposed.** Prefix the id in both places, `#<id> ` before the title, and widen the truncation budget by the prefix width so the title does not get shorter. Formatting lives in the render layer, so this is presentation, not data.

**Half of a pair — read with `EY72YA9`.** Showing an id creates references, and right now resolving one means reading the CSV by hand, which is the exact failure mode `AQQNPAN` describes. Land the lookup (`EY72YA9`) with this, not after: an id in the pane that nothing can resolve is a worse gap than no id at all. The id prefix is nearly free on its own; the pair is what removes the "no quick reference" problem.

Raised by the human 2026-09-27 after a path sweep of the Agents workspace: *"As always, tracked files should not contain full system paths."* The rule had no written home and no mechanical check, so it kept slipping — 20 occurrences across 6 tracked files before this was cleaned by hand.

**Why it matters, twice over.** A tracked file is versioned *and* synced between machines, so an absolute path is wrong in the ordinary way (it means nothing on Dreamer, gab, Xena or the LXC) and in the git way (it records one machine's layout as if it were the project's). The designated home already exists: `.agents/machine-info.md` is git-ignored *precisely* so it can hold machine-specific facts. That makes this a layering rule with a known landing place, not a matter of taste.

**Proposed check.** In the `.md` branch, flag a path-like token that starts with `/storage/`, `/home/<user>/`, `/root/`, or `~/`. Message should name the file, the line, and the landing place: *point at `.agents/machine-info.md`, or make the path repo-relative.*

**Exemptions to design for, each with a reason** — a naive check would fire on all of these:

- `.agents/machine-info.md` itself, and anything git-ignored. It is the destination, not a violation. Detection has to be "is this file tracked", not "is it a `.md`".
- `AGENTS.md` setup walkthrough — `ln -s /path/to/XLib/tools …` and an `scp -r /storage/Agents/ …` example. The machine path is the *content* there.
- Plans that describe **another** machine's layout. `plans/remote-opencode-lxc.md` is six `/root/...` paths on the LXC host, and naming them is the document's subject.
- Paths quoted as **evidence**. A model-benchmark row quotes `/home/user/project/relative/path.py` — a fictional path a model copied verbatim, cited as proof of harness defect E9. It describes no real location.

That last pair is the honest hard part: the check cannot be "contains a slash-heavy token", it has to be a deliberate judgement about whether the path is *about* something or *about where something is*. Worth writing the exemptions into the spec rather than discovering them as false positives later.

**Process.** An xlint rule gets a plan doc under `XLib/doc/plans/` and tests, like the frontmatter/fence rule — see `GBNEWPS` for the shape and `XLib/doc/plans/xlint-frontmatter-fence-skip.md`. Same file and same one-deep `.md` branch as `GBNEWPS` and `PMRBFR3`; all three should be implemented together or at least not conflict.

Suggested spec line for the rule itself, if the human wants the convention written down as well as enforced — one line in `AGENTS.md`: *tracked files name paths relative to a repo, or point at `.agents/machine-info.md` for machine locations.* The check catches the symptom; the line explains it to the agent that writes the next file.

add.issue.name: bbprs.py: blocks_the_human() ignores `state`, so a PR where the human requested changes still reports BLOCKED ON YOU

edit.description.md:
## Symptom

`bbprs.py` reports a colleague's PR as `BLOCKED ON YOU`, and `--check` exits 1,
even after the human has **requested changes** on it. Confirmed 2026-09-30 on
`mms-frontend` #79 `profile_subscription`.

The human set `changes_requested` at 07:23 UTC. The tool still reported
`BLOCKED ON YOU` on a re-run at 07:23+ and again on a later run.

This is the **inverse of the truth**. Requesting changes *completes* your review
obligation and hands the ball to the author. The tool reports it as "I might be
blocking them", so it will keep sending the human to a PR that is not waiting on
them — until that PR is approved or declined.

## Root cause

`tools/bbprs/bbprs.py:143-158`

```python
def my_participation(self) -> str | None:
    for p in self.participants:
        if p.get("user", {}).get("nickname") == HUMAN:
            role = p.get("role", "?")
            return f"{role}/{'approved' if p.get('approved') else 'NOT approved'}"
    return None

def blocks_the_human(self) -> bool:
    if self.is_mine or self.draft:
        return False
    part = self.my_participation()
    return part is not None and part.endswith("/NOT approved")
```

`my_participation()` builds its string from the **boolean `approved` only**.
`state` is never read. Bitbucket sets `approved: false` for a
`changes_requested` participant, so "I asked for changes" and "I never looked at
it" produce the identical string `REVIEWER/NOT approved` — and
`blocks_the_human()` cannot tell them apart.

## Why it matters

This is the trap the tool's own README names: *"the trap most likely to make a
tool confidently wrong rather than fail."* It is a false positive on the one
question the tool exists to answer, and it is the kind that trains the human to
ignore a `--check` that genuinely matters. A false negative is at worst a wasted
look; this one is a standing instruction to go review a colleague's PR again.

## Fix

Distinguish the three reviewer states, not two:

- `state == "changes_requested"` → the human has done their part. **Not** blocked
  on them.
- approved → not blocked (already handled).
- neither → genuinely blocked on them.

Surface `state` in `my_participation()` so the rendered output says
`REVIEWER/changes_requested` rather than the misleading `NOT approved` — the

1. **The subject format is `<REF> ` — ref, then a space.** Not `REF: `. I committed all seven branches with the git convention `VG87T14: …` and every one read as zero commits. ## The policy, as stated

- **Todo** — pending tickets.
- **In progress** — entered when it is clear how to perform them, i.e. when the human ai-oks them.
- **Done** — agents put their own tickets here when they finish.
- **Leaving Done** — the human reviews and approves; only then may an agent merge to master and delete the branch.

## The two tracks

- **Track 1 — spec pipeline.** Feature work, intent-heavy. Plan → spec (human) → tests → implementation → pass-2 review, per `doc/development.md` as it stands. Pipelined through epiq as separate commits, filed as separate tickets, driven by the human who writes the specs.
- **Track 2 — ticket as spec.** Default. Goal, requirements and decisions live in the ticket description. The implementing agent writes the tests the ticket calls for; the branch diff is the review.

1. **The subject format is `<REF> ` — ref then a space.** Not `REF: `. The matcher is `subject.toUpperCase().startsWith(ref + " ")`. I committed seven branches the git way and all seven read as zero commits; the epiq skill never states the separator.
2. **Link-by-reference reads local branches only** (`git log --branches --not <stateBranch>`). A commit needs a local branch; pushing and merging are not required for the link.

- `agent-coord.py` claims vs worktrees: `.agents/` is gitignored, so a new worktree has no `claims.json` and `check-clean` reads the shared index. Claims must resolve to the main checkout before per-ticket worktrees are safe.

add.issue.name: A patches file: durable index from commit → ticket, and the Traveller workflow it has to serve

edit.description.md:
The human's proposal, 2026-10-01, for Space Traveller and — less urgently — a repo-wide patches file. Recorded here because it is a design decision with reasoning that does not belong only in a conversation.

## As stated

- The patches file is **not densely written**: most of what a reader needs is already in epiq, and nothing is ever deleted there, so **a reference to the ticket is enough**.
- It is **updated only when a change reaches master**, and at that point the commit hashes are recorded.
- Patches are **merged to master as they come** — no batching behind a release.
- When the live server is updated, **patch notes are generated from the patches file**.

## The premise is half right, and the wrong half is load-bearing

"Nothing is ever deleted there" is correct: epiq tombstones rather than deletes, and a closed ticket stays readable. But retention is not durability, and this is measurable today:

	139 unsynced events across four ~pending.jsonl files, on this machine only

	committed log : 216 lines
	pending       : 139 lines

`0J8YBYH` — closed and merged today — appears **12 times in a pending file and 0 times in the committed event log**. Six tickets, nine comments, every lane move and that close are all one-machine-local. `epiq_sync` returns `skipped: true` and does not publish them. STATUS.md records this as `AZHG0FK`, closed 2026-09-29 as accepted risk; it is not stale, it is current and it has grown.

**So the argument inverts.** A ref in a commit subject points at a ticket that may exist only on one unsynced machine. The *reference* is the fragile thing, not the payload. What is genuinely durable here is the opposite of what the patches file was proposed to avoid depending on: the commit sha, in git, pushed.

That argues for the file more than the human's own reasoning does — but for a reason worth writing down, because it changes the file's job.

## What this implies for the file's shape

It is a **durable index**, not a summary. The board holds the reasoning; the file holds hashes and refs, in git, where they cannot be lost with a worktree prune. Two rules follow:

- **Generate it, never hand-maintain it.** Written at release time from `git log <prev>..<new> --format='%H %s'`, taking each ref off the subject, then committed. A hand-kept file drifts from git by exactly the amount nobody remembered; a generated one cannot.
- **"Updated only when a change reaches master" is fine as stated, but only because the merge is an agent's step.** Under the lane policy the agent merges, so the agent writes the entry in the same action. If a merge ever happens without the file being written, the guarantee is gone — which argues for deriving it at release rather than at each merge, if Traveller's volume is low.

For release notes to be *sliced* from the file, Traveller needs release boundaries — tags. Their workflow generates notes when the live server is updated, so the slice is `previous-tag..current-tag`.

## XLib probably does not need this

The human's own read, and it holds: XLib releases per library (`xcsv 1_0_0` … `1_1_0`), not repo-wide, and "what shipped" is per-version rather than a single release-notes stream. The use case is a live server updated in place. Worth building in Traveller; filing it here because XLib is where the board and the workflow live.

## Open, needs the human

1. Is the file **per-repo and generated at release**, or **per-merge and hand-maintained**? Above argues for generated.
2. Does Traveller tag releases? Without a boundary the notes cannot be sliced.
3. Does the 139-event pending backlog need fixing before any design leans on the board? `epiq_sync` skipping is the blocker and is not understood yet.

edit.description.md:
## Goal

A git hook that runs xlint before every commit, such that **a linter failure prevents the commit** (human, 2026-10-01).

## Current state (verified 2026-10-01)

- No `core.hooksPath`; `.git/hooks/` holds only the stock `*.sample` files. No pre-commit hook exists, and no tracked file references hooks at all.
- `tools/xlint/xlint.py` takes paths positionally, prints `path:line: rule`, and exits **1** on a violation (probed). That is all a hook needs to gate on.
- xlint is **not** on `PATH`; it must be invoked as `python3 <repo-root>/tools/xlint/xlint.py`.

## Why

Every xlint rule is currently enforced by prose (`AGENTS.md`: the tab rule, "violations are otherwise invisible until someone lints by hand") plus whoever remembers to run it. A rule nothing enforces is a rule that gets broken, and AGENTS.md already says to prefer mechanizing rules over prose. This is the enforcement point for all of them at once.

## The blocker to clear first: 114 pre-existing findings

`python3 tools/xlint/xlint.py $(git ls-files '*.py' '*.md')` exits 1 today — **114 findings across 13 files**:

| file | findings |
|------|----------|
| `tools/taskview/test/test_taskview.py` | 88 |
| `tools/taskview/test/test_taskupdate.py` | 15 |
| `tools/pybundle/test/fixtures/{stdlib,single,collision}/main.py`, `fixtures/{nested/server,alias/main}.py` | 1 each |
| `xlib_legacy/{CSV,Config,dumb_http,frac,websocket}.py` | 1 each |
| `dev/xprod/test/discrete.py` | 1 |

By rule: 74 function-definition-split, 17 double-blank-line, 12 unmerged plain imports, 7 missing final newline, 2 same-module-imported-twice, 2 space-indented.

Two clusters are not debt to fix but debt to scope around:

- The `pybundle` fixtures violate the import rules **deliberately** — they are the input the bundler is tested against. A hook that lints them blocks any commit staging one.
- `tools/taskview/test/test_taskview.py` is the most actively edited file in the repo right now (the open taskview tickets). A whole-file check fails every commit touching it on 88 findings nobody introduced.

So the hook cannot simply be switched on. Choose: clean the debt, add exclusions, or scope the check so pre-existing findings do not block. `Q93KNA9` ("exclusion mechanism for non-project code, deferred until it bites") is this biting.

## Design questions — the actual content

1. **Distribution.** `.git/hooks/` is untracked, so installing is a manual step per clone per machine. Either a tracked hook script plus an installer (`tools/hooks/pre-commit` + `tools/install-hooks.py`), or `core.hooksPath` pointed at a tracked directory. A fresh clone must have one documented command that works.
2. **Scope.** Staged files only (`git diff --cached --name-only --diff-filter=ACM`, filtered to `.py`/`.md`) is fast and matches "did this commit break it"; whole-repo is slow and lets unrelated debt block unrelated commits. Staged-only still means a pre-existing violation in a file you touched blocks you — see the table.
3. **Partial staging.** A partly-staged file gets linted as the working tree, not as the index. Document it, or lint the staged blob (`git show :file`).
4. **Exit codes.** Confirm xlint cannot exit non-zero for an internal error, or a crash masquerades as a violation and blocks commits for the wrong reason. The hook should say what failed.
5. **`--no-verify` bypasses it.** A guard rail, not a hard gate. Decide whether something unconditional (CI, or `tools/release/`) also runs xlint, so a bypass cannot reach master silently.
6. **Worktrees.** Agents work in `.claude/worktrees/<ref>-<slug>`. Hooks come from the common git dir, so one install covers them — but the hook must resolve the repo root rather than `cwd`, or it mis-targets inside a worktree.
7. **No machine paths.** The hook is a tracked file, so resolve `tools/xlint/xlint.py` relative to the repo root (AGENTS.md paths rule; see `7HP67R2`).

## Acceptance

- Staging a `.py` or `.md` with a violation fails the commit, naming file and line; a clean staged set commits with no noise.
- Works in a worktree as well as the root checkout.
- A fresh clone installs it with the one documented command, written down in one place (AGENTS.md pointers table, or the setup walkthrough).
- The 114 findings are fixed, excluded, or explicitly accepted — and the choice is recorded on this ticket.
- Check `doc/development.md` for whether the hook owes a SPEC line and tests, like other tooling.

- A staged file that xlint's own walk would ignore is handled by the decided rule, not by accident — the hook and `xlint .` agree about what is in scope.

edit.description.md:
Standing rule for how agents explain technical things to the human. New `doc/style/prose.md` + pointer row in AGENTS.md.

**Why:** the human can read AI prose fine until the topic is technical. Then "what does this do" / "explain the reasoning behind X" comes back as word salad — every word correct, no chain. Cause: the model narrates what code of that shape usually does instead of tracing this code, and drops intermediate states it considers obvious. Nothing is wrong locally, so it reads as plausible.

**Rules to encode:**
1. Cite identifiers — actual names, cited line per claim. Vague prose can't satisfy this; a model visibly breaks instead of bluffing, which is the signal.
2. Offer a trace, not a summary — step through the data showing state at each step. Summaries launder errors.
3. Mark inference separately from what was read.
4. Falsifiable framing — state what happens if X changes, and what assumption the explanation breaks on.

Also record the preference in `.agents/shared-notes.md` (it's not written down anywhere today, so it's re-explained every session), and note that the small workers (lfm-2.5-2.6b, qwen3.8-27b, nemotron-nano-omni-30b) are the wrong dispatch for explanation work.

add.issue.name: bbprs.py: should a bare PARTICIPANT (commented, no approval rights) count as BLOCKED ON YOU?

edit.description.md:
## The question

`bbprs.py` reports `BLOCKED ON YOU` when the human appears on someone else's
live PR without having approved it. That check does not look at the human's
**role**. A colleague who added the human as a plain `PARTICIPANT` — the
human commented, but holds no approval rights — is reported as waiting on
him.

## The two readings

**It should block** (today's behavior). A participant is on the PR and has
not approved, so the PR is not moving because of him. Same *kind* of signal
as an untouched reviewer.

**It should not block.** Approval authority is what makes someone a
blocker. A commenter cannot approve, so he is never the thing standing
between the PR and merge — telling him he is blocking invites him to
approve a PR he has no rights to approve.

The argument for changing it: it is the *same class* of false positive
`3EEXMRK` just fixed. A tool that over-reports builds a `--check` the human
learns to ignore, and this is the second reason it would lie.

The argument for leaving it: it is a semantics question about the tool's
central question, not a field-reading bug, and `3EEXMRK` deliberately kept
the behavior rather than changing it silently.

## Why it is not already fixed

`3EEXMRK` pinned today's behavior with
`TestBlocksTheHuman.test_participant_blocks` so the choice is visible and
reversible rather than buried in a diff. Nothing depends on the answer: the
predicate is one condition, and the test names it.

## What a fix would look like

Key `blocks_the_human()` on `role == "REVIEWER"` rather than on
"not approved", and update the two tests that currently assert the
participant case.

add.issue.comment.md:
Solution: PR #21, branch `3eexmrk-bbprs-review-state`, commit `3f2fac7`. All four acceptance criteria met, plus the test harness.

## The actual root cause was one level deeper

The ticket says `state` is never read. True, but not the whole shape of it: `blocks_the_human()` decided by asking whether the **rendered display string** ended in `/NOT approved`:

```python
part = self.my_participation()
return part is not None and part.endswith("/NOT approved")
```

So the boolean was recovered by parsing prose. Adding `state` to that string would have worked by luck, not by construction — any rewording of the label silently changes the tool's answer. The decision now reads the participant record directly (`_my_record()`), and `my_participation()` is only ever rendered.

## A second bug the ticket did not know about

Bitbucket spells "no state" as JSON `null` on some records and the **string** `"null"` on others. The string is truthy, so the obvious fix —

```python
state = record.get("state")
return f"{role}/{state or 'NOT approved'}"
```

— makes an untouched reviewer render as `REVIEWER/null` and, worse, makes
`blocks_the_human()` return **False** for a PR genuinely waiting on the
human. It would have traded one false positive for a false *negative*, and
`--check` would have gone permanently 0. `_review_state()` collapses both
spellings to one absence.

I caught this by mutation rather than by reading: the naive fix passes
every test written from the ticket's description. Reverting the original
code fails 5 tests; the naive fix fails a 6th.

## One thing deliberately not decided

A bare `PARTICIPANT` — the human commented but holds no approval rights —
still reports `BLOCKED ON YOU`, exactly as before. Whether that is right is
a semantics question about the tool's central question, not a field-reading
bug, and this ticket is scoped to the latter. I did not change it silently;
it is pinned by `TestBlocksTheHuman.test_participant_blocks` and filed as
`AMCWKQY` for you to call.

## Tests

24 offline fixture-based tests — the tool's first suite. Fixtures are shaped
like real API responses and go through `parse_pr()`, extracted from
`open_prs()` so they exercise the same mapping the live code does; a test
that hand-builds a `PullRequest` would prove nothing about what the API
sends. Each fixture carries a `_comment` naming the case it pins.

blocker rides alongside a `changes_requested` PR — the fix must not turn it

`tools/taskview/test/` has ~110 unlinted xlint violations (missing final

never to have been linted. The three files here are clean. Not fixed here;
worth a ticket if you want tool tests under the linter.

Left in **Done** per this repo's rule (finished, awaiting your review).

## The defect

`tools/xlint/xlint.py:28-31` skips any path with a part named `test`:

```python
def is_ignored(path):
	parts = set(path.parts)
	excluded = {"__pycache__", ".git", "node_modules", "xlib_legacy", "test"}
	return bool(parts & excluded)
```

The other four entries in that set are "not our code" — vendored, generated, or
foreign. `test` is the repo's own test-folder convention: `AGENTS.md` and
`doc/development.md` both rule that a test folder is `test/`, never `tests/`
(rename in progress, `2VD2XZC`). So the exclusion set skips **every test file
in this repository**, and it does so silently — `xlint .` reports zero
violations and exits 0.

## What it hides

`python3 tools/xlint/xlint.py .` → **0 violations**. The same linter pointed
at the files it skipped:

| Directory | Hidden violations |
|---|---|
| `tools/taskview/test/` | 103 |
| `tools/pybundle/test/` | 5 |
| `dev/xprod/test/` | 1 |
| `tools/bbprs/test/` | 0 |
| `tools/skynet/test/` | 0 |
| **total** | **109** |

`test_taskview.py` and `test_taskupdate.py` account for 109 of those between
them: missing final newlines, function definitions split across lines,
unmerged imports, double blank lines.

`tests/` — the name the house rules call *wrong* — is **not** in the exclusion
set, so the four libraries still using it (`dev/xconf`, `dev/xcsv`,
`dev/xschema`, `dev/xtest`) are linted today. Renaming them to the correct
`test/` as `2VD2XZC` requires would move all four **out** of lint coverage.
They are clean at present, so nothing breaks on the rename — but the fix for a
style ticket would quietly disable the check for four libraries.

That inversion is the tell: the linter is sensitive to exactly the name the
style rules mandate, and in the wrong direction.

## The decision this needs

Which did the author mean?

- **Skip foreign test data only** — then narrow it to `xlib_legacy/test` (or
  whatever the original target was) instead of the bare name `test`, and the
  109 violations become visible and get fixed.
- **Skip all tests on purpose** — then that is a rule to write down, not a
  set entry to infer, and `AGENTS.md` should say test code is exempt from
  style enforcement. Today it is enforced everywhere except where the rules
  say it applies.

- **`XCKN0AT`** (pre-commit hook running xlint on staged files) inherits this
  verbatim. Whether the hook catches a violation depends on whether it walks
  directories or lints each staged file by path — the same distinction that
  makes this invisible today.
- **`bbprs`** (`3EEXMRK`) was the first tool test written to be lint-clean, and
  it is only clean because it was linted by explicit path. A directory sweep
  or a bare pre-commit hook would not have looked at it.

```python
            role = p.get("role", "?")
            return f"{role}/{'approved' if p.get('approved') else 'NOT approved'}"
    return None

def blocks_the_human(self) -> bool:
    if self.is_mine or self.draft:
        return False
    part = self.my_participation()
    return part is not None and part.endswith("/NOT approved")
```

`my_participation()` builds its string from the **boolean `approved` only**.
`state` is never read. Bitbucket sets `approved: false` for a
`changes_requested` participant, so "I asked for changes" and "I never looked at
it" produce the identical string `REVIEWER/NOT approved` — and
`blocks_the_human()` cannot tell them apart.

The deeper shape: the boolean is recovered by **parsing the display string**.
Adding `state` to that string would work by luck rather than by construction, and
any rewording of the label would silently change the tool's answer. The decision
belongs on the participant record; the string is display only.

## Why it matters

This is the trap the tool's own README names: *"the trap most likely to make a
tool confidently wrong rather than fail."* It is a false positive on the one
question the tool exists to answer, and it is the kind that trains the human to
ignore a `--check` that genuinely matters. A false negative is at worst a wasted
look; this one is a standing instruction to go review a colleague's PR again.

## Fix

Distinguish the three reviewer states, not two:

- `state == "changes_requested"` → the human has done their part. **Not** blocked
  on them.
- approved → not blocked (already handled).
- neither → genuinely blocked on them.

Surface `state` in `my_participation()` so the rendered output says
`REVIEWER/changes_requested` rather than the misleading `NOT approved` — the
same field name is already used in `--json`, so the string is a display concern
only.

## Second defect, folded in 2026-10-01 — a bare PARTICIPANT is not a blocker

Found while verifying the fix against the live API, and folded into this ticket
rather than a separate one per the workflow's rule on tightly-coupled follow-ups.

`blocks_the_human()` never looked at the human's **role**. Bitbucket sets
`role: REVIEWER` only when you are **explicitly added as a reviewer**; anyone
who interacts with a PR otherwise appears as `PARTICIPANT`, and the author always
does. So a bare `PARTICIPANT` for the human means **he commented on a PR he was
never asked to review** — and he holds no approval right on it, so there is no
action of his that could ever clear the flag.

**Instance: `mms-frontend` #71**, "SCSS refactor to latest Dart Sass spec" (author
Raul Taremaa). Three comments from the human on 2026-08-31; never added as a
reviewer; Indrek Pertman and Toomas were, and both had approved. The tool
reported `BLOCKED ON YOU` for the two and a half weeks until it merged — naming
a blocker the human could not unblock.

Across all **225** open and merged PRs in `mms-frontend` and `mms`, the old and
new predicates disagree on that one PR and no other, so the fix is one added

- `--json` `my_participation` for #79 reads `REVIEWER/changes_requested`.
- Add a fixture-based test covering all four participant shapes
  (`approved`, `changes_requested`, reviewer-never-participated, participant).
- `bbprs.py` has **no test suite today** — the acceptance criteria above are the
  first thing that would need one, so the harness is part of the work, not a
  follow-up.

  PR — regression case `mms-frontend` #71 — while an untouched `REVIEWER` on the
  same PR still blocks.

edit.description.md:
Found 2026-10-01 while answering a question about `check-clean`'s "paths span multiple repos" error. **The guard does not fail loudly on worktree paths — it silently reports `clean` whether or not the file is dirty.** A guard that says "clean" is worse than one that errors, because the error would have been noticed.

## Mechanism

Three facts compose into the bug.

**1. `nearest_git` requires `.git` to be a directory** (`tools/agent-coord.py:791-799`):

```python
def nearest_git(path):
	base = os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(path))
	while True:
		if os.path.isdir(os.path.join(base, ".git")):
			return base
```

A git **worktree** has `.git` as a *file*, not a directory. So a path inside
`.work/<REF>-<slug>/` walks straight past the worktree root and resolves to the
**parent** repo.

**2. `cmd_check_clean` groups by that, then matches by relative path**
(`:801-825`): it runs `git status` in the resolved repo and compares
`os.path.relpath(p, repo)` against the dirty list. For a worktree path the
relative path is `.work/3EEXMRK-…/tools/bbprs/README.md`, while the parent
repo's status lists `.work/` as a single untracked directory. Nothing matches,
so the result is `clean`.

**3. `claim` and `check_clean` resolve paths differently.** `claim_paths` uses
`os.path.realpath` (`:390`), which **follows symlinks**. `cmd_check_clean` uses
`os.path.abspath` (`:803`), which does **not**. So the two commands can disagree
about which file is meant — and the asymmetry is why the symlink case is silent
too (below).

## Evidence

A file in the worktree was made dirty, then checked both ways:

```
$ printf '\n# scratch\n' >> .work/3EEXMRK-…/tools/bbprs/README.md   # uncommitted
$ python3 tools/agent-coord.py check-clean .work/3EEXMRK-…/tools/bbprs/README.md
clean                     (exit 0)   <-- the file is dirty
$ python3 tools/agent-coord.py check-clean tools/bbprs/README.md
clean                     (exit 0)
```

`git status` in the worktree confirms the edit was real. The guard saw a clean
file that was not clean.

## "paths span multiple repos" — what actually triggers it

Not the agent-file symlinks, though they are what *makes you mix repos*.

```
$ python3 tools/agent-coord.py check-clean tools/bbprs/bbprs.py /storage/Agents/AGENTS.md
paths span multiple repos: /storage/Agents, /storage/GitHub/Fun/XLib   (exit 2)
```

The error needs **two genuinely different repos in one call**. The
`.opencode/agent` symlink does not produce it: because `abspath` does not follow
symlinks, a path under `.opencode/agent/` resolves to **XLib** —

```
.opencode/agent/secretary.md  ->  /storage/GitHub/Fun/XLib
```

which is its own silent failure. `.opencode/agent/` is gitignored in XLib, so
`check-clean` on an agent file matches nothing in XLib's status and always
answers `clean`, while the file actually lives in `/storage/Agents`. Per
`AGENTS.md` the agent files are a shared symlink into the Agents workspace, so
this is a path class agents are told to edit.

## Two records describe this wrongly

- **`STATUS.md`** (Blocked) says: *"`claim` accepts a worktree path, and
  `check_clean` then refuses the same path with 'paths span multiple repos'."*
  The refusal does not happen. What happens is the silent pass above.
- **This session's own `HISTORY.md` and `.agents/shared-notes.md` entries**
  claimed the failure "did not reproduce" and that both path forms "worked".
  True, and misleading: it did not reproduce because `check-clean` was not
  checking. Recorded here rather than quietly fixed, because the correction
  belongs where the wrong claim is.

## Fix direction

Three separable things, smallest first:

1. **`nearest_git` should accept `.git` as a file** — `os.path.exists` rather
   than `os.path.isdir`. Then a worktree path resolves to the worktree, and
   `check-clean` reads the right status. This alone turns the silent pass into a
   correct answer.
2. **Make `claim` and `check_clean` agree on path resolution** — both
   `realpath`, or both `abspath`. As it stands they can name different files for
   the same argument.
3. **Decide what a path inside a symlinked foreign repo should do.** Options:
   treat it as the repo it really lives in and say so, or refuse explicitly with
   the target named. Silently checking the wrong repo is the one option not
   available.

## Why it matters here specifically

The human ruled on 2026-10-01 that epiq work happens in a worktree so the branch
at the root stops mattering. `check-clean` is the mechanism `AGENTS.md` points
at before the first edit: *"run `python3 tools/agent-coord.py check-clean <path>`
— `clean` means proceed, `dirty` means stop"*. Under the new workflow it
answers `clean` unconditionally for exactly the files agents are told to check
before editing, and a second session editing the same file is invisible to it.

edit.description.md:
The claim system (`claim` / `release` / `status` / `check-clean` in `tools/agent-coord.py`, state in the gitignored `.agents/claims.json`) existed to stop two agents editing one file in a shared checkout. A worktree per ticket makes the filesystem the boundary instead, so claims are now a second mechanism that is wrong exactly where it matters.

Measured 2026-10-01, across the eight open branches — all built in one root checkout between 19:03 and 19:45:

- `.agents/claims.json` read `{}` the whole time. No agent held any claim while the collisions below happened.
- Neither worktree has a `.agents/` directory at all, because it is gitignored. A new worktree cannot read or write claims.
- `check-clean` run from inside `.work/3EEXMRK-bbprs-review-state` returns `clean` for the file that agent was editing. `nearest_git` (`tools/agent-coord.py:791`) requires `os.path.isdir('.git')`, and a worktree's `.git` is a file, so it walks up to the root checkout and reports *its* status.

**Remove:** `claim`, `release`, `release-all`, `status`, `check-clean`, and the `check-clean` step in `AGENTS.md`'s "Working tree" section.

**Keep:** `id`, `note`, `instance-note`, `workspace`, `dispatch`, `role-*`, `personal`, `ctx`, `news`, and the lock file, which still serialises the writers that remain.

## The part worktrees do not replace

Decide this before deleting anything, or the guard is lost rather than replaced. Two agents editing the same tracked file in *different* worktrees do not collide in the checkout — they collide at merge. Live from 2026-10-01, all open, all needing hand-resolution at merge time:

| file | tickets | size |
|------|---------|------|
| `personal/Xonok/STATUS.md` | `3EEXMRK`, `58MXTGY`, `FZDMC84` | 1 conflicting hunk (3EEXMRK × 58MXTGY) |
| `tools/taskview/SPEC.md` | `EY72YA9`, `X06YVNP` | 2 hunks, both authors already cross-reference each other |
| `AGENTS.md` | `58MXTGY`, `FZDMC84` | merges clean today |

Proposed replacement for the per-file claim on shared state files: `personal/<person>/{STATUS,HISTORY,TASKS}.md` are written by the secretary **at merge time**, not carried on feature branches. That takes STATUS.md out of every branch's diff, which is where all three of tonight's conflicts came from. Needs the human's ruling — it changes what a Done ticket is allowed to contain.

Do not close `8FVW49J` as part of this. It is the prerequisite: until it lands, `check-clean` cannot be trusted even in the root checkout.

Third data point on the `skipped: true` symptom, and it does **not** reproduce it — 2026-10-03, `opencode/secretary`.

## What happened this session

| call | what preceded it | result |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | `actor_assume`, then `issue_comment_add`, then `issue_close` | `createdCommit: true`, `pushed: true`, `d5ee23d` |
| 2 | immediately after, no new write | `createdCommit: false`, `pushed: false`, **no `skipped` field** |

Both of that session's writes are in the committed log — verified by reading the events file, not by trusting the return value: `add.issue.comment` `01M40QBY…` and `close.issue` `01M3YV0CAM6ZEKB0VSC5DZ8NB1` are its last two lines, and all 4 lines of the leftover pending file are already present in it.

So: a single sync flushed two writes, and the extra drain had nothing to do and said so. Taken with the table in the previous comment, a sync called *immediately after a write* skipped 2 times out of 3 and did not skip the third.

## The reading I would change the diagnosis to

**It looks like a race, not a one-call lag.** A lag would skip deterministically on the call after a write; this skipped twice and not once, on the same sequence of steps. A pending file written by the MCP tool while `epiq_sync` is already reading is the shape that fits: the sync sees nothing new, reports success, and the next call finds the event sitting in the file it never read. It should therefore be intermittent, and worse under load — three `opencode/secretary` sessions were live this morning, all writing the same actor's log.

The practical advice is unchanged and is the part worth mechanising: **`skipped: true` is a signal to retry, not a verdict that there was nothing to do**, because it returns `status: success` and a session that walks away on it loses its last write silently. `createdCommit: false` with no `skipped` is the honest no-op and needs no retry. A drain script should loop until it sees `createdCommit: true` *or* a no-op, not sync once and continue.

## One thing the detector half should know

A drained pending file is **left on disk**, not deleted. `2cs40bjsw0d5m0a2zrw6bcdqm5~pending-…jsonl` (Sep 29) still sits beside its committed `2cs40bjsw0d5m0a2zrw6bcdqm5.jsonl` (Oct 2), byte-identical to what was committed, and my own pending file is in the same state right now. So *a pending file existing* is not a stranded signal — only its content being absent from the committed log is. Anything reporting "N stranded" off file presence will report a growing false count every time anyone drains successfully.

add.issue.name: A dev-version bypass, so a library under development can be tested against a live project

edit.description.md:
XLib has no sanctioned way for a running project to consume a library from `dev/`. Two rules combine to make it impossible by construction:

- `AGENTS.md:91` — libraries never use unversioned imports, and the only exception is a test *inside* the dev folder itself.
- `doc/library-structure.md:41-43` — dev folders are not packages; they are reached "by path, not by being a package".

So `dev/<library>/` is reachable from its own tests and from nothing else. All five dev libraries (`xconf`, `xcsv`, `xprod`, `xschema`, `xtest`) develop this way and **none has ever been exercised against a running application**.

## Why it matters

The workflow this repo exists for is: develop a library → test it where it runs → release it. XLib currently supports only the last step, so the middle one has no mechanism at all. A library can only be validated by a synthetic test, never by the application that will actually use it — which is the opposite of how the human works.

It is also blocked behind `1ZY2Q5Q`: `release.py` resolves dev folders at the wrong path, so **nothing has been releasable since 2026-09-17** (`xlib/` holds six releases, all predating the move). Until that is fixed, a bypass is not a convenience — it is the only path from a `dev/` library to a running project at all.

## What the human proposed

Symlinks inside XLib, so there is a folder holding dev-version entry points and a project can import a library from it directly, with no release in between. Still open: the folder's name and location, whether it is tracked or generated, and how `xlib/__init__.py` resolution should treat it.

## Alternatives worth choosing between

| Option | Shape | Trade-off |
|---|---|---|
| Dev symlink folder | a folder of symlinks into `dev/`; projects import from it | cheapest to build; a symlink is a tracked file carrying a path, which the repo's own path rule (`7HP67R2`) discourages |
| Pin file | extend the existing `xlib_pins` hook — `_resolve()` already looks for one, but it maps a name to a *version*, not to a dev folder | no new paths in the tree; touches the resolution path every import goes through |
| Documented `sys.path` entry | no XLib code change; the project's launcher prepends `dev/`, and `AGENTS.md:91`'s exception clause is widened to cover it | smallest change, but every consumer repeats the incantation and the import line differs between dev and released |

Whichever is chosen, the **rule change is half the work**: a mechanism with no amendment to `AGENTS.md:91` leaves the library's own AGENTS.md forbidding the thing being built.

## Concretely waiting on this

`xhttp` — an HTTP library being hand-written now in `Space-Traveller/lib/`, destined for `XLib/dev/xhttp/` once it is decent, with Traveller as the live test case. That move is blocked on this ticket: without it, `xhttp` can be released-and-pinned but never developed-against.

Two things worth keeping cheap for that move, noted here so they are not rediscovered later:

- **Write it single-file.** The bundler prefixes internal module names (`csv_tok_tokenize`), so a one-file library is completely unaffected. The constraint only bites once it is split into `_/` internals, and then the public API must be *defined* in the entry file rather than re-exported.
- **Keep reach-ins low.** What makes the move expensive is not the import line in `server.py` (one line) but every place that reaches *into* the library's request state — `server.py`, `server/Chat/api.py` and `lib/websocket.py` all do. Fewer of those is the honest measure of how well the "no bundled state" goal went, and it is what keeps the eventual move to XLib cheap.

## Related

- `1ZY2Q5Q` — `release.py` resolves dev folders at the wrong path; every release fails. The amplifier here.
- `Z491RDN` — the patches-file design, which needed to know how a release lands in git.

add.issue.name: epiq-pending: a stranded close or comment exits 0 "clean" and names no ticket — only missing creations are reported

edit.description.md:
The detector half of `FZDMC84` landed in `9a74e5b` (merged 2026-10-08). It reports **missing creations**. It does not report **missing state transitions**, which is the half that made the failure invisible for three days — and `FZDMC84`'s own thread names this as the part it closed without building.

## Reproduced, not inferred

Fixture: a ticket whose `add.issue` **is committed**, whose `close.issue` and `Solution:` comment are **only in a pending file**, pending file backdated to 10s.

```
$ python3 tools/epiq-pending.py
exit: 0
  epiq project 01PROJ: no stranded events (2 events in flight, not yet synced)
clean
```

Exit **0**, the word **clean**, while the ticket's close and its comment exist in no committed log on any machine. Backdate the same fixture to 2h and the tool does notice — it prints `2/2 events  actor bbbb…  last written 2h ago / add.issue.comment, close.issue` — but **still names no ticket**, where the creation-loss half prints `created only here: ISSUE1  xlint frontmatter rule`.

## The asymmetry is the bug

`_pending_report` (`tools/epiq-pending.py:106`) builds `row["created"]` by filtering `_kind(e) == "add.issue"` (`:122`), and `_print_rows` (`:139`) is the only thing that turns an id into a human-readable subject. So:

| loss | reported | ticket named? |
|------|----------|---------------|
| creation stranded | orphan section, `created only here:` | yes |
| close / comment / move stranded | stranded count + kinds | **no** |

`CREATING_KINDS` vs `REFERENCING_KINDS` (`:6-8`) already draw the line: `close.issue`, `add.issue.comment`, `move.node`, `edit.title`, `edit.description`, `add.issue.tag` are all referencing kinds, so an event of any of them can be stranded while its target's creation is perfectly committed — and the tool has no vocabulary for that at all.

## Why the second row is the dangerous one

This is `GBNEWPS`, quoted from `FZDMC84`'s thread: `epiq_issue_get` returned it **closed with a `Solution:` comment** and `QN1N82Y` as a **filed ticket in Todo** — both sourced from the on-disk pending file, neither in any committed log. A fresh clone therefore had **no `QN1N82Y` at all**, and had `GBNEWPS` **open in Todo with no `Solution:` comment**: an implemented, spec-backed xlint rule reading as work never started. Neither reads as an orphan. Both read as *fine*, from the only machine that has the data.

The stranded-count split is deliberate and I am not asking to remove it — `FZDMC84` records why: a check that fires on the calling agent's own unsynced writes every session is a check that gets ignored. The problem is that the carve-out's subject is a **count**, and a count without a subject cannot be triaged. An agent reading `2 events in flight` has no way to learn that one of them is the close of a ticket it believes is shipped.

## What would falsify this

If a clone of the state branch can be shown to *preserve* pending events — i.e. durability does not in fact depend on the commit — then the whole framing is wrong and the tool is correct to ignore mutations. Nothing I know contradicts that, but I have not tested it, and it is the premise the ticket rests on.

## Scope

- Name the affected issue for stranded `REFERENCING_KINDS` events, not only `add.issue` — reuse `_issue_titles`, which already reads pending files (`tools/epiq-pending.py:58`) so a subject resolves even when the creation is stranded too.
- A second report that names the **divergence**, not the loss: for each stranded referencing event, what a clone sees versus what this machine sees. That is the report `FZDMC84` promised and did not deliver.
- Keep the age-based in-flight/st-stranded split as it is. Tests in `tools/test/`, per `doc/development.md`.

- `FZDMC84` — closed 2026-10-08; this is its undelivered half, recorded on the ticket before closing.
- `AZHG0FK` — the accepted-risk ruling this supersedes.
- `AK633QC` — a linter reporting 0 over content it should have flagged; same shape, different tool.

add.issue.name: Add xlib_dev override: run real code against an unreleased library

edit.description.md:
`from xlib_dev import xcsv` resolves a bare name to `dev/xcsv/xcsv.py` instead of the newest file in `xlib/`, so one import line is the only change between testing a prerelease and testing what users get.

Resolved through `__getattr__` rather than a file per library: adding a library needs no change, and the caller gets the real module object rather than a copy of its names taken at import time. The library keeps its own module name, so `dev/xcsv/xcsv.py:31`'s `from ._ import csv_tok,csv_ser` still resolves.

**Covers the caller's import only.** A library's own imports of other libraries stay pinned to released versions, which the libraries-are-pinned rule requires — testing a dev xcsv still gets a released xschema. A dev library depending on another dev library is fine and intended; only the dev to release boundary is policed, and by release.py refusing to package the library.

**Not a release.** The dev surface is a superset: internals appear as themselves (`xcsv.csv_tok`) where the bundle renames them (`xcsv.csv_tok_tokenize`). Passing through `xlib_dev` is not proof of passing against the release that follows.

Enforcement is separate: xlint repo-specific rules, the `xlib_dev` rule itself, and release.py refusing a dev dependency are filed as their own tickets.

add.issue.comment.md:
Solution: `xlib_dev/__init__.py` resolves any name backed by a `dev/<name>/<name>.py` through a module-level `__getattr__`, aliasing the real module into `sys.modules` so relative imports inside the library still resolve. Chosen over a file per library: adding a library then needs no change, and the caller gets the module object rather than a name snapshot. Verified from a project outside the repo that swapping one import line moves the load between `dev/xcsv/xcsv.py` and `xlib/xcsv_1_1_0.py`. 12 tests in `xlib_dev/tests/`, mutation-checked — breaking the import target fails 4 of them. Committed `b0214a4` on master, epiq ref `ASTXNPG`.

Two limits worth keeping in view, both documented in `doc/library-structure.md`:

- It covers the caller's import only. A library's own imports of other libraries stay pinned to released versions, so a dev xcsv under test still gets a released xschema. Dev-to-dev is fine and intended; only the dev-to-release boundary is policed, and that belongs to release.py.
- It is not a release. The dev surface is a superset — `xcsv.csv_tok` where the bundle emits `xcsv.csv_tok_tokenize` — so passing through `xlib_dev` is not proof of passing against the release that follows.

One test here already enforces part of what the enforcement tickets cover: `test_no_released_file_references_the_override` scans `xlib/*.py` for the string. When the lint rule lands it should move there rather than be duplicated.
